paragraphs: R' Yitzchak bar Elyashiv. Hyman describes him as a great man and a wonder-worker, of the fourth generation in Eretz Yisrael, as is related of him in Taanit 23b: that R' Mani (the son of R' Yonah) used to frequent R' Yitzchak bar Elyashiv, and told him that the wealthy men of his father-in-law's household were distressing him. He said, "Let them become poor"—and they became poor. [R' Mani] said to him, "They press me" (that they ask me for sustenance). He said, "Let them become rich"—and they became rich. He said:

"My wife is not pleasing to me" (that his wife was not beautiful). He said to him, "What is her name?" "Hannah." "Let Hannah become beautiful"—and she became beautiful. He said to him, "She is acting haughtily toward me" (she will become proud toward me). He said to him, "If so, let Hannah return to her dark [former] state"—and so it was. He also had two students who asked him to beg for mercy on their behalf that they might become wise; he refused, and said to them: "It was with me, and I sent it away."

He is mentioned in Sukkah 19a, and in the Yerushalmi there, chapter 1, halakhah 11, he resolves the difficulty of Rav Oshaya and R' Abba. He is likewise mentioned in Berakhot ch. 7 halakhah 1 and Maaser Sheni ch. 2, end of halakhah 2. His death we find in Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 3:1: when he died, seventy איתקופין (the precise term remains unresolved) of the householders of the Galilee were uprooted; they said that they had been sustained by his merit. And in Moed Katan 25b: when Rabbi Elyashiv died,

seventy burglary tunnels were opened, and the reading in Ein Yaakov is "R' Yitzchak bar Elyashiv." Hyman reports that in Yuchasin it is written that he lived in the time of R' Yochanan; perhaps what was written was ר״י, and that is R' Yonah.

notes.text: The named Davidson Taanit23b has Mani finding his wife unpleasing, then complaining of her haughtiness after her beauty changed. The reply It was with me, but I sent it away alludes to the capacity he had renounced, not an identified woman.

Moed Katan25b in that edition has the shorter Rabbi Elyashiv and seventy burglary tunnels in Nehardea; Hyman reports a fuller name in Ein Yaakov. The precise Yerushalmi term איתקופין remains unresolved. Hyman’s proposed Yonah rather than Yochanan remains his conjecture.
